title: Few questions during reading
statement: Keep questions during reading few and at natural breaks, because frequent ones can cut young readers' recall of what they don't ask about.
example: In one study, Grade 4 recall of untargeted information fell from .30 with no questions to .07 with questions during reading.
detail: A research-boundary review checked a cited experiment in which 240 students, 60 each in Grades 4/7/10 and college, met 14 written causal questions per story during reading, after reading or not at all (Van den Broek et al. 2001, https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-0663.93.3.521; `grade3-reading/artifacts/feedback-devfactory-2026-09-10/analysis-current-courses/RESEARCH-BOUNDARIES.md`, section 2). The quoted fall from .30 to .07 is Grade 4 recall of untargeted information, not overall comprehension, and the college benefits concerned targeted information. The review concludes that frequent unsupported interruptions can be costly for younger readers, and that a change of timing should compare equal-content versions and measure both whole-story understanding and targeted learning.
against: After-reading questions also lowered that recall (.16 against .30), readers could not look back while answering, and the review says the study does not establish a ban on every mid-text check, especially sparse checks at coherent boundaries with the text available (the same file, lines 27-31).

evidence.quote: **14 written causal questions per story** appeared during reading, after reading, or not at all.
The quoted **.30 control → .07 during-reading** result is Grade4 recall of **untargeted information**, not overall comprehension.
**Design conclusion:** frequent unsupported interruptions can be costly for younger readers.

Van den Broek and colleagues tested 240 children in the equivalents of Year 4, Year 7, Year 10 and undergraduates, asking questions during and immediately after reading, and found that "it was the youngest pupils whose comprehension and recall suffered the most from questions asked both during and immediately after reading."
Are we asking so many questions that the kids are kind of missing the point?
